As someone exploring modern web development, backend technologies, and AI-powered applications, I’m especially interested in seeing how Appwrite continues to make application development simpler and more accessible.

Home robots are coming — and they may start much smaller than we expect.

Pollen Robotics, the robotics team at Hugging Face, has just opened pre-orders for Microduck, a $399 open-source bipedal robot.

At just 25 cm tall and around 800 g, Microduck packs some impressive hardware:
• 15 motors
• Wide-angle camera
• ToF LiDAR
• 2 IMUs
• An articulated beak for picking up objects
• 7 trained behaviors out of the box
And the really interesting part?

It is built to be programmable and trainable.

Pollen Robotics has released the SDK, simulator, robot software, and reinforcement-learning training stack openly on GitHub, allowing developers to experiment with new behaviors and train policies in simulation before deploying them to the real robot.

That changes the idea of a “home robot.”

It isn't just a device that performs a fixed set of commands.

It becomes a small physical platform for experimenting with AI, reinforcement learning, robotics, and sim-to-real learning.

The future of robotics may not begin with giant humanoids in every home.
It could begin with small, affordable, programmable robots that people can actually experiment with.

$399. Open source. Trainable. Physical AI in your hands.
What would you teach Microduck to do?

Architecting AI Agents: It’s More Than Just an LLM

AI agents are moving from simple chatbots to systems that can reason, use tools, make decisions, and complete tasks autonomously.

But building a reliable AI agent isn’t just about connecting an LLM to a prompt.

It’s about designing the right architecture.

In this video, I explore the core ideas behind Architecting AI Agents, including:
→ How different components work together
→ The role of tools, workflows, and decision-making
→ Handling failures and unexpected outcomes
→ Designing reliable agentic systems
→ Moving from a simple AI response to an autonomous workflow
→ Why architecture matters for scalable AI applications

A powerful model alone doesn’t make a powerful agent.
The architecture around the model does.

The future of AI is not only about better models.

It’s about building systems that can think, act, adapt, and execute.

What do you think is the most important component of an AI agent architecture?

AI doesn’t really “remember” you. So how does AI Memory work?
We often use AI assistants and assume they remember everything we’ve told them.
But there’s an important difference:
Context ≠ Memory
Context is what the AI can see in the current conversation.
Short-term memory is information temporarily retained to continue a task or conversation.
Long-term memory is information intentionally stored and retrieved later.
For an AI agent, memory can become much more powerful.
Imagine telling an AI:
“I prefer Python over JavaScript.”
Later, you ask:
“Suggest a project for me.”
A memory-enabled agent could use your previous preference and recommend a Python project.
That creates a completely different experience.
A simple AI Memory architecture:
User
↓
AI Agent
↓
Memory Layer
↓
Store important information
↓
Retrieve relevant memories
↓
Generate personalized response
But there’s a bigger challenge:
What should an AI remember?
It shouldn't store everything.
A good memory system needs:
• Relevance
• Retrieval
• User control
• Privacy
• Expiration and deletion
• Context awareness
I believe AI Memory will become one of the most important building blocks of agentic AI.
The future isn't just:
“AI that can answer.”
It's:
“AI that understands, remembers, learns from interactions, and knows when to use what it remembers.”
Should AI assistants remember everything, or only what we explicitly allow them to remember?

🚀 Learning by Building: Elastic User Group Gujarat Workshop
Had a great experience attending the Elastic User Group Gujarat Workshop in Ahmedabad! 🤝

The hands-on session, “Build Agentic Workflows and Searchable Apps with Elasticsearch, Jina, and Agent-to-Agent Communication,” was a fantastic opportunity to explore how modern AI systems can combine search, embeddings, and autonomous agents.

A few key things I learned:
🔹 Elasticsearch for intelligent & semantic search
🔹 Jina Embeddings for converting data into searchable vectors
🔹 Elastic Agent Builder for creating agentic workflows
🔹 A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol for communication between AI agents
🔹 How these technologies can come together to build real-world AI-
powered searchable applications
What I especially enjoyed was the code-along, practical approach — not just learning the concepts, but actually understanding how the different pieces of the modern AI stack fit together. 💻🤖

Events like these are a great reminder that the best way to understand emerging technologies is to build, experiment, and learn with the community.

Big thanks to everyone who organized and contributed to this amazing session! 
Someshwaran M | Shiv Jani | Dhairya Panchal | Rachana Chauhan | Harshvardhansinh Jadeja
